unresolvedReferences.description: 宅皋狼: Mengzeng is called Zhai Gaolang (commentators read 宅 'resided at' the place Gaolang); the next unit uses 皋狼 as his name, so both are kept as alternate names.
The two Qiangjiuru women and Zhao Shuai's Jin wife are unnamed here; they are kept as unnamed persons.
The crown prince's mother (Duke Xiang's consort) is unnamed here.
置兒叱罅 appears corrupt (received texts read 置兒絝中, 'placed the child in her trousers'); translation left unrepaired pending the source text.
吾先君 'our former lord' who judged Zhao Dun guiltless is taken to be Duke Cheng of Jin.
屠岸賈 is romanized both Tu An Jia and Tu'an Gu in the draft; same person.
趙氏復位十一年 (c. 571 on the Shiji count from 582) conflicts with the independently established date of Duke Li's killing of the three Xi (574); the event is dated 574 as strongly inferred.
The text calls Zichao King Jing's younger brother (弟); he is recorded as the text states.
The child seen at the Emperor's side is interpreted as Jianzi's son (later Zhao Wuxu/Xiangzi); he is not named in this chunk and is not linked.
The Fan-Zhonghang rising is dated here to Duke Ding's 14th year (498), with the Handan events the next year (497); the chunk's dates follow the Shiji sequence.
荀櫟 (Xun Li) is identified with 知伯文子 / 知伯 (Zhi Wenzi) of s0224/s0230 as the same Zhi-clan head; strongly inferred.
The chapter places Yue's destruction of Wu in 475 (是歲, Duke Ding's last year) and has Yue besieging Wu again in Xiangzi's first year (s0258); recorded as stated.
Duke Chu of Jin's flight and death is dated here by Xiangzi's fourth year (454), whereas the chapter's own Duke Chu 17th year (458) marks Jianzi's death; recorded as stated.
The 'strong king' (伉王) of the prophecy is an unnamed future ruler and is not linked.
The draft renders 桓子 (Huanzi) as 'Jianzi'; the surface is linked to Huanzi and a repair is proposed.
The chapter places Marquis Wen of Wei's death in Duke Wu's 13th year (387); recorded as stated.
虜其太子、痤 is punctuated in the packet as two captives (the crown prince and Cuo); some editions read one person.
大戊午 (Da Wuwu, 334 BC) may be the same man as the chancellor 太戊午 (Tai Wuwu, 372 BC) of the previous chunk; kept distinct here.
The general Zhao He (趙何) of 312 BC predates and is distinct from the later King Huiwen, whose personal name is also He.
天子 (the Son of Heaven, i.e. the reigning Zhou king) is not named and is disposed as a title.
The Chinese reads 公字成, evidently a scribal error for 公子成 (Prince Cheng); linked as Prince Cheng.
我先王 'my former kings' is plural/generic (Wuling's forebears) and is not linked to one person.
King Wu of Qin's death is placed in King Wuling's 18th year (308) by this chapter.
Li Dui's warning to Fei Yi is undated; placed after Zhang's enfeoffment (296) and before the crisis, 296-295, as strongly inferred.
The Chinese reads 主主開之, evidently a scribal error for 主父開之 ('the Lord Father opened the gate').
The princess (公主) who died in 286 is not otherwise identified.
The chapter places Bai Qi's victory at Huayang in King Huiwen's 25th year (274 BC by this chronology); other records date the Huayang battle to 273 BC.
s0652-s0660 continue the persuader's letter (attributed to Su Li in the preceding chunk); the author is not named within this chunk, so no author claim is repeated here.
The Changping campaign, Zhao Kuo's surrender and the siege of Handan are narrated after year 4 without a year number; other records date Changping to 260 BC. Dated here only as between years 4 and 8.
Zhao Sheng (s0762) is identified with the Lord of Pingyuan (s0759, s0774) on the conventional identification; the text itself does not equate them explicitly.
Zhao Bao, Lord of Pingyang, is kept distinct from the earlier Zhao Bao, Lord of Yangwen.
The Lord of Chang'an enfeoffed with Rao in 239 may be the queen dowager's son sent as hostage in 265; the text does not say, so he is kept as a separate person.
Pingdu (平都) appears to be a person (perhaps a Lord of Pingdu) held with or instead of the Lord of Chunping; the identity is unclear.
徒父祺出 'Tu Fuqi went out' is obscure; neither the person nor the event is explained.
King Daoxiang's death is recorded after his ninth year without an explicit year number.

s0850a-s0850h are the rhymed appraisal verse (Suoyin shuzan, a later commentary) appended to the chapter; the persons named there are treated as retrospective references, dated only from the earlier narrative.
King Qian's surrender (以王遷降) is recorded after the 7th-year events and before the fall of Handan in the 10th month of the 8th year; dated here as 229-228.
Jia's reign in Dai is given only as six years after Qian's capture; dated approximately 228-222.
